claims.source: In both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutant mice the differences in vivo in SS firing frequency between lobules I–III and lobule X were still significant, analogous to that in normal mice (a6-Cacna1a, I-III: 75.1 ± 19.0 Hz, X: 50.2 ± 10.2 Hz, t = 3.979, p<0.001; PC-Δγ2, I-III: 89.8 ± 14.9 Hz, X: 60.9 ± 15.6 Hz, t = 4.876, p<0.001) (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The CV2 values of SS activity were significantly reduced not only in vitro, but also in vivo in both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutants as compared to wild-types.
claims.source: In contrast, the CV2 values of SS activity were significantly reduced not only in vitro, but also in vivo in both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutants as compared to wild-types (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The SS firing frequency is largely determined by intrinsic properties of PCs, whereas the level of regularity appears to be predominantly determined by external inputs.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that the SS firing frequency is largely determined by intrinsic properties of PCs, whereas the level of regularity appears to be predominantly determined by external inputs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data from in vitro recordings and mutant mice.

claims.claim: When the products of aldolase C (GAP and DHAP) were introduced to the ACSF in in vitro recordings, SS firing increased in both lobule III and lobule X.
claims.source: In fact, when the products of aldolase C, that is glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), were introduced to the ACSF in our in vitro recordings, SS firing increased in both the largely zebrin-negative lobule III and zebrin-positive lobule X (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), arguing against the possibility that aldolase C's enzymatic function directly contributes to a lower SS firing frequency in Z+ PCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Both TRPC3 blockers (genistein and Pyr3) had a significant impact on PC activity reducing the firing frequency in lobule III without a significant effect in lobule X.
claims.source: Both TRPC3 blockers had a significant impact on PC activity reducing the firing frequency in lobule III (genistein, p<0.001; Pyr3, p<0.001 vs vehicle control, one-way followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) without a significant effect in lobule X (p=0.271 and p=1.000 vs vehicle respectively, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) (Figure 6A,B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings with TRPC3 blockers shown in Figure 6A,B.

claims.claim: Wash-in of Pyr3 had a robust effect on SS firing frequency of PCs in lobule III and this effect was significantly larger than that in lobule X.
claims.source: Wash-in of Pyr3 had a robust effect on SS firing frequency of PCs in lobule III (pre: 49.9 ± 7.9 Hz; post: 25.5 ± 9.9 Hz; t = 5.412, p=0.002, paired Student's t test) and this effect was significantly larger than that in lobule X (reduction, lobule III: 48.2 ± 19.7%; lobule X: 8.5 ± 16.6%; t = 4.069, p=0.002) (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from wash-in experiments shown in Figure 6D,E.

claims.claim: Blocking EAAT4 in vitro had no significant effect on the activity of Purkinje cells in either lobule III or lobule X.
claims.source: Based on the higher expression of EAAT4 in Z+ Purkinje cells, blocking EAAT4 would arguably affect lobule X more than lobule III, but the general EAAT blocker DL-TBOA had no significant effect on the activity of Purkinje cells in either lobule (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B) (lobule III: t = 1.219, p=0.227; lobule X: t = −0.597, p=0.533)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings with EAAT4 blocker shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In vivo, both genistein and Pyr3 caused a decrease in SS activity in lobules I–III, while no significant effect was recorded in lobule X.
claims.source: In line with the in vitro data, both genistein and Pyr3 (i.p. and i.c.v., 240 mg/kg and 200 µg, respectively) caused a decrease in SS activity in lobules I–III, lasting for several hours (vehicle: 90.6 ± 13.3 Hz; genistein: 74.6 ± 14.9 Hz; Pyr3: 61.6 ± 15.5 Hz; both p<0.001 vs vehicle, One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test), while no significant effect was recorded in lobule X (vehicle: 52.9 ± 13.3 Hz; genistein: 57.5 ± 20.8 Hz,; Pyr3: 51.1 ± 14.3 Hz, p=0.546 and p=0.887 vs vehicle, One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) (Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings with TRPC3 blockers shown in Figure 6F,G.

claims.claim: TRPC3 contributes to the elevated SS activity in zebrin-negative PC zones.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that TRPC3 contributes to the elevated SS activity in zebrin-negative PC zones.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data with TRPC3 blockers.

claims.claim: This study provides the first evidence for ubiquitously organized differences in cerebellar Purkinje cell firing activity in vivo.
claims.source: This study provides, to our knowledge, the first evidence for ubiquitously organized differences in cerebellar Purkinje cell firing activity in vivo and for the correlation of these differences to a marker protein, zebrin II.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of their findings in the context of existing literature.

claims.claim: Purkinje cells within the same module operate around a preferred range of intrinsically determined SS firing frequencies.
claims.source: As zebrin, as a biomarker, can be associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit (Brochu et al., 1990; Voogd et al., 2003; Pijpers et al., 2006; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007), our results indicate that Purkinje cells within the same module operate around a preferred range of intrinsically determined SS firing frequencies and that this activity is different from modules with a different zebrin identity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations about modular organization.

claims.claim: CS activity is altered as a secondary effect of differences in SS activity.
claims.source: Moreover, presumably as a secondary effect, CS activity is also altered.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlated changes in CS activity.

claims.claim: The difference in SS firing frequency is probably largely determined by the intrinsic properties of PCs.
claims.source: The difference in SS firing frequency is probably largely determined by the intrinsic properties of PCs, as this difference was maintained in the reduced slice preparation, in which the inputs are blocked, as well as in mouse mutants, in which the excitatory (a6-Cacna1a mice) or inhibitory (PC-Δγ2 mice) inputs are attenuated.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in reduced preparations and mutant mice.

claims.claim: The level of regularity of firing (CV2) was not consistently dependent on zebrin identity, but significantly altered by impairing the excitatory and/or inhibitory inputs.
claims.source: In contrast, the level of regularity of firing (i.e., CV2) was not consistently dependent on zebrin identity, but significantly altered by impairing the excitatory and/or inhibitory inputs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice and in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: Reduction of simple spike frequency in lobule III in vivo for several minutes to hours by Pyr3 application also reduced complex spike frequency.
claims.source: In fact, reduction of simple spike frequency in lobule III in vivo for several minutes to hours by Pyr3 application also reduced complex spike frequency, supporting the indirect control of simple spikes on complex spike activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings with Pyr3 application.

claims.claim: Temporary increases in climbing fiber-evoked CS activity suppress SS frequency providing a homeostatic control mechanism within an olivocerebellar module.
claims.source: Interestingly, temporary increases in climbing fiber-evoked CS activity suppress SS frequency providing a homeostatic control mechanism within an olivocerebellar module (Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing homeostatic mechanisms.

claims.claim: External inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation.
claims.source: Thus, whereas the external inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation (Badura et al., 2013; Galliano et al., 2013), their intrinsic properties appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest, around which they can operate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations.

claims.claim: Intrinsic properties of PCs appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest.
claims.source: Thus, whereas the external inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation (Badura et al., 2013; Galliano et al., 2013), their intrinsic properties appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest, around which they can operate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules.
claims.source: It should be noted that, although TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules (Allen Brain Atlas, www.brain-map.org), there is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in protein levels (Hartmann and et al, 2008; Becker et al., 2009; Sekerkova et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Allen Brain Atlas and citations.

claims.claim: There is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in TRPC3 protein levels across the cerebellum.
claims.source: It should be noted that, although TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules (Allen Brain Atlas, www.brain-map.org), there is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in protein levels (Hartmann and et al, 2008; Becker et al., 2009; Sekerkova et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining TRPC3 protein expression.

claims.claim: The differential effect of blocking TRPC3 suggests that its activity might be higher in Z− PCs.
claims.source: If the expression of TRPC3 is indeed homogeneous throughout the cerebellum, the differential effect of blocking TRPC3 suggests that its activity might be higher in Z− PCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data with TRPC3 blockers.

claims.claim: Zebrin II or aldolase C bears the capacity to bind IP3.
claims.source: In fact, zebrin II or aldolase C, which is not likely to be involved via its enzymatic function, bears the capacity to bind IP3 (Baron et al., 1999), and thus could potentially reduce the activation of TRPC3 in Z+ PCs, through the IP3-receptor.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baron et al., 1999.

claims.claim: mGluR1 can be tonically activated.
claims.source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing mGluR1 function.

claims.claim: mGluR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency.
claims.source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing mGluR1 blocker effects.

claims.claim: mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers.
claims.source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing TRPC3 blocker effects on mGluR1-evoked currents.

claims.claim: The low and high baseline frequencies of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs appear to be in line with their propensities for induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), respectively.
claims.source: Interestingly, the low and high baseline frequencies of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs also appear to be in line with their propensities for induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), respectively (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations about plasticity mechanisms.

claims.claim: Entrainment of cerebellar nuclei neurons by synchronized SS input from PCs may occur at 50–80 Hz, but is impaired at 100 Hz.
claims.source: Likewise, entrainment of cerebellar nuclei neurons by synchronized SS input from PCs, which results in phase-locking of connected neurons, may occur at 50–80 Hz, but is impaired at 100 Hz (Person and Raman, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Person and Raman, 2012.

claims.claim: The cerebellar nuclei can be divided based on the zebrin expression pattern, with a rostral half that receives, predominantly, input from zebrin-negative PC's and a caudal part that mostly receives zebrin-positive inputs.
claims.source: The cerebellar nuclei can also be divided based on the zebrin expression pattern, with a rostral half that receives, predominantly, input from zebrin-negative PC's and a caudal part that mostly receives zebrin-positive inputs (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007; Sugihara et al., 2009; Sugihara, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the organization of cerebellar nuclei.

claims.claim: PC input to cerebellar nuclei neurons may be segregated on the basis of frequency.
claims.source: This implies that PC input to cerebellar nuclei neurons may be segregated on the basis of frequency, and that as a consequence the output of cerebellar nuclei neurons located within zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative territories may be distinctly different.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and anatomical organization.

claims.claim: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of SSs and CSs and the consistent presence of a pause in SS firing after a CS (climbing fiber pause).
claims.source: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of SSs and CSs and the consistent presence of a pause in SS firing after a CS (i.e., climbing fiber pause) (Figure 1C–F).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological criteria used to identify Purkinje cells in recordings.

claims.claim: Of the 104 PCs included in the analysis, 47 and 57 cells were located in Z− and Z+ zones, respectively.
claims.source: Of the 104 PCs included in the analysis (50 mice), 47 and 57 cells were located in Z− and Z+ zones, respectively (Figure 1G, plot adapted from Sugihara and Quy, 2007).
claims.evidence: This describes the sample size and distribution of recorded cells.

results.result: Purkinje cells in zebrin-negative (Z−) modules exhibit significantly higher simple spike (SS) firing frequencies (~96 Hz) compared to zebrin-positive (Z+) modules (~61 Hz), with correspondingly longer climbing fiber pauses in Z+ cells. This difference is consistently observed across all transverse zones of the cerebellar cortex and is linked to zebrin identity rather than lobular location.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C21-C26, C28, and C71 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (immunostaining identification, two-photon imaging in EAAT4-eGFP mice, recordings across transverse zones) with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, correlations) and adequate sample sizes (n=104 PCs from 50 mice). The consistency across different recording locations and identification methods strongly supports this core finding.

results.result: Simple spike firing frequency and climbing fiber pause show robust correlations with zebrin staining intensity across cerebellar lobules (vermis: r=0.893, p=0.007 for firing frequency; r=-0.929, p=0.003 for CF pause), while CV2 regularity does not consistently correlate with zebrin intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 demonstrate strong correlations between zebrin intensity and firing parameters across lobules with significant p-values. The data are supported by Figure 3 showing gradual changes in zebrin expression from lobule I to X. However, the correlation analysis relies on averaged lobular data which may mask within-lobule variability.

results.result: Complex spike (CS) activity differs between Z+ and Z− Purkinje cells, with Z+ cells showing lower CS frequency (0.92±0.28 Hz vs 1.13±0.25 Hz), longer half-width, larger spike area, and distinct post-CS simple spike response patterns. The suppression and oscillation response types occur predominantly in Z+ zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 and C52 provide comprehensive characterization of CS differences with statistical support (t-tests, chi-squared tests). The mechanistic interpretation (C30, C52) that CS changes are secondary to SS activity differences is supported by circuit connectivity knowledge and experimental data (C55), though the causal relationship could be more directly tested.

results.result: The difference in simple spike firing frequency between Z+ and Z− Purkinje cells is largely determined by intrinsic properties rather than synaptic inputs, as demonstrated by persistence of frequency differences in vitro (with blocked synaptic transmission) and in mutant mice lacking excitatory (a6-Cacna1a) or inhibitory (PC-Δγ2) inputs. In contrast, firing regularity (CV2) is predominantly determined by external inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43, C53-C54 provide strong evidence through multiple complementary approaches: in vitro recordings with synaptic blockers, genetic manipulations affecting specific inputs, and intrinsic excitability measurements. The correlation between in vitro and in vivo patterns (r=0.916, p=0.010) and persistence of frequency differences in mutants support the intrinsic mechanism. The dissociation between frequency (intrinsic) and regularity (input-dependent) is well-demonstrated.

results.result: TRPC3 channel activity contributes to the elevated simple spike activity in zebrin-negative Purkinje cells. Pharmacological blockade of TRPC3 with genistein and Pyr3 selectively reduces firing frequency in predominantly Z− lobule III (by ~48%) but not in Z+ lobule X, both in vitro and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46, C48-C49, C61 demonstrate selective effects of TRPC3 blockers on Z− cells with appropriate controls and statistical tests. The use of two different blockers (genistein and Pyr3) strengthens the conclusion. The wash-in experiments (C46) provide direct evidence of the effect. However, genistein is noted to be less selective, and the interpretation that TRPC3 activity (rather than expression) differs between zones (C61) is inferential.

results.result: Blocking EAAT4 with DL-TBOA had no significant effect on Purkinje cell firing frequency in either lobule III or lobule X in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is supported by experimental data with appropriate statistical tests showing no significant effects (lobule III: t=1.219, p=0.227; lobule X: t=-0.597, p=0.533). This negative result helps rule out EAAT4 as a mechanism for the observed frequency differences.

results.result: Reduction of simple spike frequency in lobule III by Pyr3 application also reduced complex spike frequency, supporting indirect control of simple spikes on complex spike activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by experimental observations during Pyr3 application. This finding is consistent with known circuit connectivity (C30) where reduced PC activity leads to disinhibition of cerebellar nuclei and subsequent inhibition of inferior olive. However, the causal relationship is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Background on cerebellar anatomy, zebrin expression patterns, and associated molecular markers. Zebrin (aldolase C) is expressed in specific bands of Purkinje cells with complementary expression of mGluR1b and similar expression to EAAT4. Several proteins in the mGluR1-TRPC3 cascade show zebrin-like expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C20 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of cerebellar organization and molecular markers, though they do not constitute novel findings of this study.

results.result: This study provides the first evidence for ubiquitously organized differences in cerebellar Purkinje cell firing activity in vivo that correlate with zebrin expression, indicating that Purkinje cells within the same module operate around a preferred range of intrinsically determined firing frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 represent the authors' interpretation of the novelty and significance of their findings. The claim of being "first" (C50) is difficult to verify without exhaustive literature review, but the comprehensive nature of the data across the entire cerebellar cortex supports this assertion. The conclusion about modular organization (C51) is well-supported by the experimental data and citations about zebrin-module relationships.

results.result: External inputs to Purkinje cells control precise temporal coding and dynamic range during stimulation, while intrinsic properties determine baseline firing frequencies at rest. Temporary increases in climbing fiber activity can suppress simple spike frequency, providing homeostatic control.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 integrate the current findings with prior literature (supported by citations). The distinction between input-dependent temporal coding and intrinsic baseline frequencies is well-supported by the experimental data from this study (C43, C53-C54). However, these claims extend beyond the direct experimental observations to propose functional interpretations.

results.result: TRPC3 gene expression varies across lobules but protein levels appear homogeneous. Zebrin/aldolase C can bind IP3, potentially modulating TRPC3 activity. mGluR1 can be tonically activated and its blockers reduce firing frequency, with mGluR1-evoked currents blocked by TRPC3 inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60, C62-C65 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims provide mechanistic context for interpreting the TRPC3 blocker results. The apparent contradiction between gene expression gradients (C59) and homogeneous protein levels (C60) is acknowledged by the authors and leads to the inference about differential TRPC3 activity (C61).

results.result: The differential baseline frequencies of Z+ and Z− Purkinje cells may relate to their propensities for LTP and LTD, affect entrainment of cerebellar nuclei neurons (optimal at 50-80 Hz), and potentially lead to frequency-based segregation of PC input to cerebellar nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 propose functional implications of the observed frequency differences. While C66-C68 are supported by citations to relevant literature, C69 is explicitly speculative ("may be segregated"). These claims extend beyond the direct experimental observations to propose testable hypotheses about downstream consequences. The functional significance requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of simple spikes, complex spikes, and consistent climbing fiber pause.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 describes standard methodological criteria for identifying Purkinje cells in electrophysiological recordings. This is well-established methodology supported by the data shown in Figure 1C-F.
